items.q: A database is described as a collection of related data representing some aspect of the real world. What is that slice of the real world called?
options: The mini-world, or Universe of Discourse (UoD)
items.explain: The portion of the real world a database models is the **mini-world** or **Universe of Discourse (UoD)**. Deciding where its boundary falls is the first act of database design.

items.q: Which is NOT one of the three properties that make a collection of data a database?
options: It is logically coherent, with inherent meaning
It is designed, built and populated for a specific purpose
The data within it is related
It is stored on a single centralised server
items.explain: Storage location is irrelevant to the definition — distributed databases exist. The defining properties are **related** data, **logical coherence**, and being built **for a specific purpose**.

items.q: In the DBMS function 'defining', what exactly is produced and where is it kept?
options: The data itself, kept on the storage medium
Metadata describing types, structures and constraints, kept in the DBMS catalog
Query execution plans, kept in the buffer pool
Access permissions, kept in the operating system
items.explain: **Defining** specifies data types, structures and constraints; that description is **metadata** stored in the **DBMS catalog**. This is the self-describing nature of a database system.

items.q: A data model is a collection of conceptual tools for describing which four things?
options: Data, data relationships, data semantics and consistency constraints
items.explain: The standard definition names **data, data relationships, data semantics, and consistency constraints**. Dropping semantics or constraints is the usual way marks are lost.

items.q: Which workload is characterised by a large number of users performing small retrievals and updates?
items.explain: **OLTP (Online Transaction Processing)** — many users, small reads and writes; typical of banking, universities and airlines. OLAP processes data to draw conclusions and build predictive models.

items.q: Loan approval, targeted advertisements and manufacturing decisions are given as examples of which mode of database use?
items.explain: These are **OLAP / analytics** applications — processing data to draw conclusions and build predictive models. Data mining combines AI and statistical techniques for this.

items.q: MongoDB is named as an example of which category of database application?
items.explain: **Document databases** store semi-structured data as JSON/BSON/XML with flexible schemas and horizontal scaling. MongoDB is used by *The New York Times* for news and media content.

items.q: According to Ramakrishnan & Gehrke, how does a semantic data model differ from a data model?
options: A semantic data model is what the DBMS implements directly
A semantic data model is more abstract and higher-level, easing initial description; it is then translated into the DBMS's data model
A semantic data model describes only physical storage
There is no difference; the terms are synonyms
items.explain: A **semantic data model** (like the **ER model**) is more abstract, designed for humans to describe an enterprise. A DBMS is typically built around a data model with few basic constructs (relational), so the semantic design is **translated** into it.

items.q: In the university scenario, adding a new major requires creating new permanent files AND writing new application programs. What underlying defect does this reveal?
options: The structure of the data lives inside the programs, welding data and programs together
items.explain: In a file-processing system the data's structure is embedded in application code, so a change in the mini-world forces a change in program code. The purpose of a DBMS is to separate the two — **program–data independence**.

items.q: A student enrolled in a double major has their details stored once per department. Which drawback is this, and what problem does it cause beyond wasted space?
options: Data redundancy; possible data inconsistency when one copy changes
items.explain: **Data redundancy** wastes storage AND risks **data inconsistency** when only some copies are updated. The DBMS fix is a centralised store so changes are made at a single spot.

items.q: Account A holds ₹10,000. Two clerks concurrently deduct ₹500 and ₹100; both read 10,000 before either writes. What are the possible final balances, and what is the correct one?
options: 9,500 or 9,900 depending on who writes last; correct is 9,400
items.explain: Both read 10,000, compute 9,500 and 9,900 respectively, and the **last writer wins** — so the balance ends at 9,500 or 9,900 instead of the correct **9,400**. This is the **lost update** anomaly.

items.q: Transferring ₹5000 from A to B debits A but crashes before crediting B. Which drawback is this, and which DBMS feature solves it?
options: Atomicity problems; transactions with automatic rollback
items.explain: This is the **atomicity** problem: either both steps happen or neither. The DBMS provides **transactions** and **automatic rollback** on failure.

items.q: 'Each department's research-fund balance must stay above 0' is coded into every application program. Which drawback is this?
items.explain: **Integrity problems** — the constraint lives in code, so adding a new one means editing every program. The DBMS lets you declare constraints **in the schema**, enforced automatically; adding one means updating the schema only.

items.q: Payroll personnel can accidentally see and change academic records because programs accumulated with no central security. Which drawback is this?
items.explain: **Security problems.** The fix is access controls and permissions defined by an administrator and enforced **at the database level, regardless of which application program is used**.

items.q: A business runs separate inventory and order systems; inventory is not updated in real time from sales, so it oversells. The lecture classifies this as which problem type?
items.explain: The lecture's answer is **data isolation** — two related systems that are not integrated, so neither sees the other's state. The tell is *'separate systems'*, not *'at the same time'*. Look for the phrase naming the **cause**, not the damage.

items.q: Which characteristic of the database approach means the system stores a complete definition of the database structure and constraints alongside the data?
items.explain: The **self-describing nature** — the system holds the database *and* its complete description (**metadata**) in the catalog. The other three characteristics are built on top of this one.

items.q: 'A view may be a subset of the database or it may contain virtual data derived from the database files but not explicitly stored.' Which characteristic is this?
options: Support for multiple views of the data
items.explain: **Support for multiple views.** The key phrase is **virtual data derived from the files but not explicitly stored** — views are computed on demand.

items.q: Which advantage of database systems refers to making program objects persist beyond program execution?
options: Providing persistent storage for program objects
items.explain: **Providing persistent storage for program objects** — e.g. object-oriented DBMSs make program objects persistent, avoiding the conversion normally needed to save an in-memory object to a file.

items.q: Which kind of integrity guarantees that a reference points to something that actually exists?
items.explain: **Referential integrity** — every enrolment must refer to a valid student. Entity integrity is unique identifiability; domain integrity is permitted values; user-defined integrity is business rules.

items.q: Why does data abstraction exist at all, according to the lecture's chain of reasoning?
options: Efficiency forces complex data structures, but many users are not computer trained, so complexity is hidden behind layers
To comply with the ANSI standard
To allow multiple users to connect concurrently
items.explain: The chain: retrieval must be **efficient** → efficiency demands **complex data structures** → many users are **not computer trained** → developers **hide the complexity** behind layers of abstraction.

items.q: At which level of abstraction are the RELATIONSHIPS between entities described?
items.explain: The **logical level** describes what kind of data is stored **and how different pieces of information are related to each other** — e.g. 'Students belong to Departments'. Omitting relationships is the standard way this definition is under-answered.

items.q: Changing from sequential to random-access files without altering the conceptual schema is an example of what?
items.explain: **Physical data independence** — modifying the physical schema (storage devices, data structures, indexes, file organisation) without altering the conceptual/logical schema.

items.q: Adding new attributes to the Department entity without changing application programs demonstrates which property?
items.explain: **Logical data independence** — modifying the logical schema (inserting/deleting attributes, altering table structures, entities or relationships) without affecting external schemas or applications.

items.q: Which kind of data independence is harder to achieve, and why?
options: Physical, because storage hardware changes frequently
Logical, because application programs are written directly against the logical structure and name its tables and columns
Neither is difficult in a relational DBMS
items.explain: **Logical** data independence is harder. Applications depend heavily on the logical structure, so insulating them from logical change is only ever partially achievable — while physical independence is near-total in modern relational systems.

items.q: In the programming analogy, the database schema corresponds to what?
options: The values of variables at a point in time
Variable declarations together with their type definitions
items.explain: **Schema ≈ variable declarations + type definitions**; **instance/state ≈ the values of the variables at a particular point in time**.

items.q: Immediately after a new database is defined to the DBMS, what is its state?
options: The initial state, containing default rows
The empty state, with no data
Undefined until a query is run
A copy of the previous database's state
items.explain: When we define a new database we specify **only the schema**; the corresponding state is the **empty state**. The **initial state** arrives when the database is first populated or loaded.

items.q: Which statement about the number of schemas in a database is correct?
options: Exactly one of each: conceptual, physical and external
Exactly one conceptual and one physical schema, but possibly several external schemas
Several conceptual schemas but one physical schema
One external schema and many conceptual schemas
items.explain: There is **exactly one conceptual and one physical schema** (there is just one set of stored relations), but **several external schemas**, each tailored to a group of users.

items.q: In the three-schema architecture, which mapping delivers logical data independence?
options: No mapping does; it comes from the conceptual schema itself
items.explain: The **external/conceptual mapping** gives **logical** data independence; the **conceptual/internal mapping** gives **physical** data independence. The mappings are the whole point of the architecture.

items.q: Why is a view's data computed on demand rather than stored?
options: Because storing it would be redundant, and redundancy invites inconsistency
Because the SQL standard forbids storing views
Because views have no primary key
items.explain: Storing a derivable view wastes space and risks inconsistency — e.g. an enrolment could be inserted without incrementing a stored enrolment count. **Derive what you can, store only what you must.**

items.q: In the database design diagram, the dashed line separating DBMS-independent from DBMS-specific work falls between which two phases?
items.explain: The **conceptual schema is DBMS-independent**; the **logical schema is expressed in the data model of a specific DBMS**. So the dashed line falls between **conceptual design and logical design**.

items.q: Requirements collection and analysis splits into which two streams?
items.explain: It splits into **functional requirements** (→ functional analysis → transaction specification → application programs) and **data requirements** (→ conceptual → logical → physical design → internal schema).

items.q: Which DBMS module writes metadata into the system catalog?
items.explain: The **DDL compiler** processes schema definitions and **stores the metadata in the catalog**. The query optimizer and DML compiler **read** from it — that asymmetry is the self-describing nature turned into wiring.

items.q: Which module extracts DML commands from an application program?
items.explain: The **pre-compiler** extracts DML commands from the application program, passing them to the **DML compiler** and the remainder to the **host language compiler**.

items.q: In the component-modules diagram, which class of user reaches compiled transactions WITHOUT passing through a compiler at request time?
items.explain: **Parametric (naïve) users** run **canned transactions** compiled in advance — which is why a booking screen is fast. Casual users pay the compile-and-optimise cost on each interactive query.

items.q: Which database system utility includes data conversion tools from an old format to the new database format?
items.explain: The **loading utility** loads existing data files into a database and **includes data conversion tools** from the old format to the new one.

items.q: Which utility monitors database usage and provides statistics to the DBA?
items.explain: **Performance monitoring utilities** monitor usage and provide statistics to the DBA — the input for tuning decisions.

items.q: A system runs on a tightly-coupled cluster with many cores, shared memory and shared disk, for large-scale data warehousing. Which architecture?
items.explain: **Parallel** databases run on a cluster of machines with many cores, shared memory and shared disk, for high-performance workloads. NASA's HPC handling of satellite data is the lecture's example.

items.q: Which architecture stores data across multiple physical or geographic locations, gaining fault tolerance through replication?
items.explain: **Distributed.** Parallel is about *one system going faster* in one place; distributed is about *data living in many places*, gaining scalability, fault tolerance and performance.

items.q: In a two-tier architecture, client programs send query and transaction requests via which standard interfaces?
items.explain: **ODBC** (Open Database Connectivity) and **JDBC** (for Java). Both client and server must install the appropriate ODBC/JDBC module.

items.q: How does the three-tier architecture enhance security relative to two-tier?
options: The database server is accessible only via the middle tier; clients cannot access it directly
It stores no data on the client
items.explain: The **database server is only reachable through the middle tier**. In two-tier every client holds database credentials; in three-tier the client holds application credentials, replacing N trust relationships with one.

items.q: The three tiers are also named by layer. Which is the correct set?
options: Interface Layer / Logic Layer / Storage Layer
Presentation Layer / Business Logic Layer / Database Services Layer
External Layer / Conceptual Layer / Internal Layer
Client Layer / Network Layer / Server Layer
items.explain: **Presentation Layer / Business Logic Layer / Database Services Layer**, corresponding to Client / Application (Web) Server / Database Server.

items.q: 'Application programmers are responsible for defining storage structures and access methods in the database.' True or false?
options: True — they design the physical layout
False — the Database Administrator handles this
items.explain: **False.** Storage-structure and access-method definition is a **DBA** function. Application programmers write the *programs that use* the database; the DBA defines the *database itself*.

items.q: Which type of user would most likely use a query language to retrieve specific data from a database?
items.explain: **Sophisticated users** possess deep DBMS understanding and are proficient with **DDL and DML** commands — data engineers and developers issuing SQL directly.

items.q: Booking a movie ticket through an app makes you which kind of database user?
items.explain: A **naïve (parametric end) user** — you interact through a **predefined interface** without needing to know anything about how the database works.

items.q: Which is NOT one of the five listed functions of a Database Administrator?
options: Writing the application programs used by end users
Routine maintenance including backups and performance monitoring
items.explain: Writing application programs is the **application programmer's** job. The DBA's five functions are schema definition; storage structure and access-method definition; schema and physical-organisation modification; granting authorization; and routine maintenance.

items.q: Which of these is an entity with CONCEPTUAL (abstract) rather than physical existence?
items.explain: A **university course** is conceptual, as are a company, a job, a project and a reservation. Cars, persons, employees and houses have **physical** existence. Both kinds serve equally as distinct objects.

items.q: What does the EXTENSION of an entity set refer to?
options: The unique identifier for each entity
items.explain: The **extension** is the **actual collection of entities** at a point in time — part of the *state*. The entity **type** (name + attributes) is part of the *schema*.

items.q: Formally, an attribute A of entity set E with value set V is defined as a function A : E → P(V). Why the power set P(V) rather than V?
options: To allow attribute names to repeat
So one definition covers single-valued (singleton), multivalued (larger set) and null (empty set) cases
items.explain: Mapping into **P(V)** lets one formula describe all three cases: single-valued → a **singleton**, multivalued → a set with several elements, null/not applicable → the **empty set**.

items.q: When is modelling an attribute as COMPOSITE the right choice?
options: Whenever the attribute is a string
When a user will sometimes refer to the whole attribute and sometimes to only a component of it
Only when the attribute is also multivalued
When the attribute is derived from another
items.explain: The stated design rule: composite is a good choice **if a user will wish to refer to the entire attribute on some occasions, and to only a component on other occasions** — e.g. wanting the postal code alone out of an address.

items.q: How is a multivalued attribute drawn in an E-R diagram?
items.explain: **Double ellipse** = multivalued. **Dashed ellipse** = derived. **Underlined** name = key. **Double rectangle** = weak entity.

items.q: In the schema Instructor(ID, Name, Department, Date_of_Birth, Age), what is the design problem?
options: Age is derivable from Date_of_Birth and should not be stored
ID is not a valid key
Name should be simple, not composite
items.explain: **Age is a derived attribute** — computable from Date_of_Birth and the current date. Storing it is not merely redundant; it becomes wrong within a day. R&G call `age` an explicit example of poor design.

items.q: In the notation Address_EmPhone({Email}, {Phone}, Address{House, number, street, City, State}), what do the braces around Email and Phone indicate?
items.explain: **Braces = multivalued.** The grouped component list `Address{...}` is **composite**, and the whole nested structure is a **complex attribute**.

items.q: PreviousDegrees of a Student is denoted {PreviousDegrees(College, Year, Degree, Field)}. What type of attribute is it?
options: Complex — nesting of composite and multivalued
items.explain: Multiple values can exist (**multivalued**) and each has four subcomponents (**composite**) — the nesting of the two makes it a **complex attribute**.

items.q: VehicleTagNumber is a key of the CAR entity type with components (Number, State). What does this illustrate?
options: That keys must be simple attributes
That a key attribute may be composite, and that an entity type may have more than one key
items.explain: A **key may be composite** — a plate number alone is not unique across states. CAR also has a second key, **VehicleIdentificationNumber (VIN)**, showing an entity type may have **more than one key**.

items.q: How does key underlining differ between an ER diagram and a relational schema?
options: In an ER diagram EVERY key is underlined; in a relational schema only ONE primary key is underlined
In an ER diagram no key is underlined
In a relational schema every candidate key is underlined
items.explain: **Each key is underlined** in an ER diagram — so two underlined attributes on one entity means two candidate keys, not an error. When reducing to a relational schema you must **choose one** primary key.

items.q: A null value for an apartment number could carry which three distinct meanings?
options: Not applicable; missing (exists but unknown to us); unknown (we don't know whether it exists)
items.explain: **Not applicable** (the value does not exist), **missing** (it exists but we lack the information), and **unknown** (we do not know whether it exists). Null is not zero and not the empty string.

items.q: In the Environmental Sensor exercise, a sensor 'collects multiple Data readings, each containing a Date-Time and a Value'. How is Data modelled?
options: A complex attribute — multivalued (double ellipse) and composite (Date-time, Value)
items.explain: *'Multiple'* → **multivalued** (double ellipse); *'each containing'* → **composite** components Date-time and Value. Together: a **complex attribute**. Sensor_ID is the underlined key.

items.q: Instructor Katz (ID 45565) advising student Shankar (ID 12345) is an example of what?
items.explain: A **relationship instance** — a specific association between **named entities**. The general definition `advisor` relating `instructor` to `student` is the relationship **set/type**.

items.q: Which is an example of a recursive relationship?
items.explain: **Course prerequisites** — the only option where **both ends are the same entity set** (`course` to `course`). The other three join two different entity sets.

items.q: Why are explicit role names NECESSARY in a recursive relationship set?
options: Because the same entity set participates more than once, so without labels you cannot tell which end is which
Because recursive relationships have no key
Because they must always be ternary
items.explain: The pair `(CS201, CS101)` is meaningless until the lines are labelled `course_id` and `prereq_id`. Roles are optional when entity sets are distinct, but **mandatory** when they are not.

items.q: The degree of a relationship set is defined as what?
options: The number of entity sets that participate
The number of attributes on the relationship
items.explain: Degree counts **entity sets**: binary = 2 (most relationship sets in a database system), ternary = 3, n-ary in general.

items.q: Why can proj_guide (instructor, student, project) NOT be replaced by binary relationships?
options: Because ternary relationships are always more efficient
Because a student could have different instructors as guides for different projects, which binary relationships cannot capture
Because binary relationships cannot have attributes
items.explain: The stated justification: **a student could have different instructors as guides for different projects**. The three-way fact is not the sum of its two-way projections.

items.q: Where should the 'Grade' attribute be placed for a Student–Enrolls–Course relationship?
options: As a descriptive attribute on the Enrolls relationship (an oval connected to the diamond)
items.explain: A grade exists **only if the student enrolled** in that course, so it belongs to the relationship. Descriptive attributes are drawn as an **oval connected to the diamond**.

items.q: In the SUPPLY ternary relationship among SUPPLIER, PART and PROJECT, what is 'Quantity'?
options: A descriptive attribute on the SUPPLY relationship
items.explain: **Quantity** is a descriptive attribute on the **SUPPLY** diamond — it only has meaning once a supplier, part and project are connected.

items.q: Which test distinguishes a relationship attribute from an entity attribute?
options: Whether the value exists for the entity on its own, or only once two entities are connected
Whether the value can be null
items.explain: A student has a **name** whether or not they enrol (entity attribute); a **grade** only in the context of a course (relationship attribute). Same for *hours per week* on a project and a manager's *start date*.

items.q: Cardinality and participation differ how?
options: They are two names for the same constraint
Cardinality says HOW MANY an entity may relate to; participation says WHETHER EVERY entity must relate at all
Cardinality applies to entities, participation to attributes
Participation applies only to ternary relationships
items.explain: **Cardinality** = 1:1, 1:N, N:1, M:N. **Participation** = total (double line) or partial (single line). They are independent, and a full specification states **both**.

items.q: A line labelled Student—Enrolls (2, 5) means what?
options: Each student enrols in a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 5 courses
The relationship has degree between 2 and 5
There are 2 total and 5 partial participants
items.explain: In (min, max) notation, l = 2 and h = 5: each student participates in **between 2 and 5** relationship instances. l ≥ 1 also implies **total** participation.

items.q: Which cardinality ratio MUST become a table of its own when reduced to a relational schema?
items.explain: **M:N** must become its own relation holding both keys. 1:N puts a foreign key on the 'many' side; 1:1 puts a foreign key on either side — preferably the side with **total participation**.
